text:
Predicates:
SpillsFoodClothes(x) ::: x spills a lot of food on his clothing.
NotablyTidy(x) ::: x is notably tidy.
ClumsyFoodie(x) ::: x is a clumsy foodie.
GoesOutFrequent(x) ::: x goes out frequently to find new food restaurants.
Cleanly(x) ::: x is cleanly.
ValuOrderSpotlessness(x) ::: x values order and spotlessness.
FamilyPrioritizeOrderSpotlessness(x) ::: x's family prioritizes order and spotlessness.
Peter ::: Peter.
Premises:
∀x (SpillsFoodClothes(x) → ¬NotablyTidy(x)) ::: If people spill food on clothes, they are not notably tidy.
∀x (ClumsyFoodie(x) ∧ GoesOutFrequent(x) → SpillsFoodClothes(x)) ::: Clumsy foodies who go out frequently spill food on clothes.
∀x (Cleanly(x) → NotablyTidy(x)) ::: Clean people are notably tidy.
∀x (ValuOrderSpotlessness(x) → Cleanly(x)) ::: Valuing order and spotlessness implies being cleanly.
∀x (FamilyPrioritizeOrderSpotlessness(x) → ValuOrderSpotlessness(x)) ::: Families that prioritize order and spotlessness influence individuals.
Peter is a person who spills food on clothes and is cleanly, or a person who does not spill food on clothes and is not cleanly. ::: (SpillsFoodClothes(Peter) ∧ Cleanly(Peter)) ∨ (¬SpillsFoodClothes(Peter) ∧ ¬Cleanly(Peter))
Conclusion:
(ClumsyFoodie(Peter) ∧ GoesOutFrequent(Peter)) ∨ FamilyPrioritizeOrderSpotlessness(Peter) ::: Peter is either a clumsy foodie who goes out frequently or his family prioritizes order and spotlessness.
